proposals.relationship: Colley uses Hobsbawm’s account of national bonding against outsiders and his rejection of cultural homogeneity to frame British nation making.
proposals.evidence_note: Selected primary 1992 article opens with Hobsbawm’s1990 formulation p.309; more substantively p.316n. 18 identifies Hobsbawm pp.1–45 alongside Sahlins as the reasons for rejecting an integration/homogenization model. Colley then analyzes shared war,Protestantism and empire. This is a specific conceptual resource, not complete theoretical agreement or a claim to have freshly read Hobsbawm’s book.

primary_locators.passage: Epigraph and paragraph beginning More broadly, plusn. 18.

proposals.relationship: Colley takes up Pocock’s expanded British-history agenda and his account of Britain’s post-imperial relation to Europe.
proposals.evidence_note: Primary pp.312–313 explains both the Four Nations gains and Pocock’s wider white-empire programme; p. 328 explicitly uses his observation that Britain can no longer control or avoid Europe,n. 53. Colley’s criticism of a narrowed Four Nations reception is not assigned to Pocock himself: she stresses that his original programme was geographically wider. UnderlyingPocock 1975/1982 articles unread.

primary_locators.passage: Pocock discussion and later explicitly attributed use,n. 7,n. 53.

proposals.relationship: Colley uses Brewer’s account of war, fiscal bureaucracy and expanding armed forces to connect state formation with British national identification.
proposals.evidence_note: Primary pp.321–322 explicitly says Brewer has shown how recurrent war strengthened the state; n. 36 identifies The Sinews of Power (1989). Colley distinguishes the established fiscal-military argument from her more tentative question about military service and popular solidarity, which she says is little researched. No automatic agreement on all dimensions and no fresh book reading.

primary_locators.passage: Paragraph beginning The fear and actuality; n. 36.

proposals.relationship: Colley draws on Said’s account of the Orient as Europe’s contrasting image to explain empire’s role in British self-definition.
proposals.evidence_note: Selected primarypp.324–325 quotes and develops Said’s relation of Orient/West; nn. 45–46 identify Orientalism (1978), 1–2, 33–34. This is a specific resource in1992, compatible with her later particular objection about early British-Muslim relations as reported by Davis. Said’s whole book is not freshly read.

primary_locators.passage: As Edward Said has remarked; nn. 45–46.

proposals.relationship: Davis reports Colley’s objection that early British-Muslim captivity and commerce complicate a sequence from degrading stereotypes to imperial domination.
proposals.evidence_note: Explicit named mediation: Davis’s 2003 reviewsection 2,paragraph beginning Colley makes some interesting comparisons and following two paragraphs, explains her rejection of the relevant Said sequence: Islam was associated with threats to Britons, Catholic rivals were more immediate enemies, and commerce/scholarship made British discourse on Islam multifaceted. This bounded contextual objection is retained alongside her 1992 use of Said. Captives and Said originals unread; no claim to have independently adjudicated all Orientalism.

primary_locators.passage: Colley makes some interesting comparisons; Not only was Islam; Moreover.

proposals.relationship: As Breuilly explains, Colley uses Anderson’s imagined political community to treat Britain as an invented nation overlying older loyalties.
proposals.evidence_note: Named scholarly mediation, Breuilly’s signed contribution acceptedpp.16–17 reproduces Colley’s 2003Pimlico wording and interprets the use. His qualification is essential: Colley moves from imagined community to invented nation and does not thereby adopt Anderson’s whole print-capitalism argument. Original1992and2003book bodies unread; no full-theory influence claim or claim based on citation frequency.

primary_locators.passage: Colley quotation and two analytical paragraphs explaining selective use.

proposals.relationship: Colley praises Pagden’s comparative study of imperial ideas but argues that commerce, conquest and global interaction exceed its Eurocentric account.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 1996 review’s final Pagden section, especially final two paragraphs. She challenges exclusion of Dutch imperialism and the chronology of British militarism inIndia, then argues that wider global interactions are needed to explain continued conquests despite metropolitan criticism. Praise for innovative comparison and classical-ideology analysis coexists. Marshall’s separately reviewed collection is not confused with Pagden’s book; book itself unread.

primary_locators.passage: One problem, as Pagden; Pagden is right of course.

proposals.relationship: Pagden praises Captives but disputes Colley’s claim that the world remains imperial while becoming post-colonial.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2002 review final substantive objection and preceding praise. He argues that colonies persist while an empire requires incorporation and reciprocal cultural change, and that American global bases alone do not meet this definition. This remains Pagden’s dated 2002 judgment, not our current geographical or political classification,and is not proof of a direct reply to Colley’s 1996 review. Captives unread.

primary_locators.passage: But for all that, Colley is surely wrong; final commendation.

proposals.relationship: Davis praises Captives while questioning its distinctions among forms of bondage, its treatment of the American Revolution and its emphasis on Britain’s smallness.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2003 review: section 2paragraphs beginning Colley should have done more and Professor Robert C. Davis distinguish slavery/captivity and warn against benign servitude; section 3 paragraph beginning While Colley succeeds challenges omission of Black revolutionary soldiers; final paragraph questions repeated smallness. His praise of complexity and Mediterranean chapters,and his earlier objection about omitted imperial legacies,remain explicit. These are David Brion Davis’s specific reservations,not neutral proof that Colley’s overall book is wrong. Robert C. Davis is a different cited scholar; no substitution. Book unread.

primary_locators.passage: Slavery/captivity distinction; revolutionaryAmerica; final smallness paragraph; praise retained.

proposals.relationship: Cozens reads Colley’s nation-in-arms argument as a challenge to Thompson’s class-centered account of working-class formation.
proposals.evidence_note: Explicitly Cozens’s 2016 reconstruction pp.12–13: he describes an implicit double challenge,questioning representativeness of the industrial workers highlighted by Thompson and foregrounding common armed service/national culture. Hisp. 15 also records Colley’s concessions of uneven discontent and contested patriotism. Neither Britons nor The Making has been freshly read; Cozens cites Colley 2009 fourth edition (original 1992) and Thompson 1991 fourteenth edition (original 1963). Claim does not say Colley denies class or all conflict.

primary_locators.passage: Implicit double-pronged attack paragraph and Colley concessions.

proposals.relationship: Thompson questions whether volunteer evidence establishes Colley’s broad loyalist consensus and argues that national unity can coexist with class division.
proposals.evidence_note: Fresh selected 1993 archival OCR includes skepticism about majority participation,volunteer humbug, and explicit compatibility of one British nation with two class nations; OCR snippets are reordered and not image-collated. Cozens 2016 pp.15–16,n. 32 independently reconstructs the precise volunteer-evidence and ambivalence objection,citing review p. 378. His explicit praise of Colley’s clear prose, stimulating study and exceptional illustrations is retained; no blanket rejection and no claim the whole original print review has been read.

primary_locators.passage: Anchors As to how far; The point is valid; The disposition of the majority; Not only were the British.

proposals.relationship: Colley includes Edmund Morgan among the scholars whose different historical fields broadened her outlook and prompted new topics.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2016 written interview opening global-outlook answer names Jonathan Spence, Edmund Morgan, John Blum and DavidBrion Davis,then explicitly credits learning from different scholars with new topic ideas. The individual edge retains that collective acknowledgment: it supplies no particular borrowed concept,sole influence or advisor claim. Demos’s subsequent lunch conversation—not this group as a whole—is the separately reported genesis of Captives. Shared Yale employment or friendship alone is not the basis.
